claims.text: Adding nanoscale WS2 particles to a high-temperature ceramic matrix composite enables stable self-lubricating behavior from ambient temperature to at least 600°C.
Adding nanoscale WS2 does not significantly compromise the mechanical strength of the ceramic composite relative to an equivalent composite without WS2.
The initial ceramic matrix composite is fully densified and contains no solid-lubricant additives.
A suitable matrix can be Si3N4 or Al2O3.
The proposed WS2 addition is 1–5 wt.% and is uniformly dispersed during powder processing before sintering.
The intended operating and test range is room temperature to 600°C in normal atmosphere.
WS2 particles form lubricant films on the contact surfaces during sliding.
The ceramic matrix supports the WS2-derived lubricant films.
At elevated temperatures, WS2 forms a low-shear layered structure on the sliding surfaces.
The low-shear WS2 surface structure reduces friction and wear.
The ceramic matrix preserves mechanical integrity and dimensional stability at elevated temperatures.
The WS2-containing composite has lower and more stable friction coefficients than the lubricant-free baseline over 25–600°C.
The WS2-containing composite has lower wear rates than the lubricant-free baseline over 25–600°C.
The addition of WS2 causes less than a 10% reduction in flexural strength.
A ceramic composite without a solid-lubricant additive exhibits higher friction and wear at elevated temperatures under otherwise identical test conditions.
Lubrication efficiency may degrade above the oxidative-stability limit of WS2, identified as above 600°C.
Phase changes in the ceramic matrix may degrade lubrication efficiency.
Shock loading or extreme thermal cycling may impair performance.
The upper operating-temperature limit and optimum WS2 fraction depend on ceramic composition and test environment.
